summary:
As of July 2026 Vermont is listed among the most protective states on gender-identity nondiscrimination. State law bans discrimination based on gender identity in employment, public accommodations, education, housing, credit, insurance and union practices. The provision was added after a 2006 veto, passed again in 2007, was signed by Governor Jim Douglas on 22 May 2007 and took effect on 1 July 2007. For a visitor the public-accommodations coverage is the operative part: hotels, restaurants, shops and service providers fall under it.

Hate-crime law provides additional penalties for an offence committed because of the victim's gender identity, added in 1999 to a 1990 statute that originally covered sexual orientation. The gay and trans panic defence was abolished and repealed by legislation that passed the House 144-1 in March 2021 and the Senate 29-0 in April 2021, was signed by Governor Phil Scott on 5 May 2021 and took effect on 1 July 2021.

Single-user public bathrooms have had to be marked gender-neutral since 1 July 2018, under a bill signed in May 2018.

Vermont's shield laws, enacted in 2023 and 2024, are enforceable against out-of-state action and place the state among those protecting transgender and non-binary people who travel in for gender-affirming healthcare; the 2023 measure took effect immediately by emergency clause.

Partner recognition is settled. Civil unions were introduced in July 2000 as the first state status identical to marriage, following a 1999 Vermont Supreme Court ruling on equal marriage benefits, and marriage for same-sex couples has been legal since 1 September 2009, the first state to adopt it through the legislature and governor rather than a court decision.
tangentialFactors:
Vermont's sexual-orientation protections run alongside the gender-identity provisions and predate them. Discrimination based on sexual orientation in employment, public accommodations, education, housing, credit, insurance and union practices was banned with protections added in 1992; hate-crime legislation covering sexual orientation was enacted in 1990; and benefits for same-sex partners of state employees have been provided since 1994.

Vermont's sodomy statutes are repealed. The penalty was reduced from capital punishment to life imprisonment in 1861; a 1937 law punished participation in oral sex with one to five years in state prison and applied to heterosexual and homosexual activity alike; that statute was repealed in April 1977; and adult private consensual non-commercial sodomy is unenforceable under Lawrence v. Texas.
localsOnly:
Gender-marker changes on Vermont birth certificates and other state-issued documents are available to both preoperative and postoperative transgender people on court order, supported by a letter from a licensed medical or mental health practitioner documenting surgical, hormonal or other appropriate treatment. Since 1 July 2022, people born in Vermont may change the sex marker to male, female or X by self-determination, without court order, mental health diagnosis, surgery, divorce or medical permission, under H.628 (Act 88), approved 6 April 2022, which amended 18 V.S.A. § 5112 to allow issuance of a new birth certificate reflecting gender identity.

The Department of Motor Vehicles has offered X on driver's licences and state IDs since 1 July 2019, with no documentation required.

Health insurers underwriting in Vermont have been required to cover transgender care, including sex reassignment surgery, since 2013.

Conversion therapy on minors, including transgender minors, is prohibited. S.132 (Act 138) was signed on 25 May 2016 and took effect on 1 July 2016, treating performance of the practice on minors as unprofessional conduct under 18 V.S.A. §§ 8351-8353 and related 26 V.S.A. licensing statutes. The bill passed the Senate unanimously on 17 March 2016, was approved with amendments in the House on 26 April and accepted by the Senate on 29 April.

Adoption and parentage rules are open to LGBT residents. Single LGBT individuals and same-sex couples may petition to adopt; lesbian couples have access to in vitro fertilisation, with the non-genetic, non-gestational mother recognised as legal parent of a child born via donor insemination irrespective of marital status; and in June 1993 the Vermont Supreme Court ruled in favour of a lesbian seeking to adopt her partner's two biological sons.

The anti-bullying law prohibits bullying, including cyberbullying, and harassment based on gender identity and sexual orientation in all educational institutions. In October 2023 the Department of Education unanimously passed a policy to protect and defend transgender and non-binary students within schools and classrooms. In 2023 Mid Vermont Christian School's girls' basketball team forfeited a match against a team fielding a transgender girl, citing fairness and safety, and the Vermont Principals' Association barred it from competition as a result.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not itemise the provisions of the 2024 shield law; the inventory records only that shield laws were enacted in 2023 and 2024 and are enforceable against out-of-state action.

No Vermont-specific enforcement data is present in the sources for the gender-identity hate-crime provision or for complaints brought under the public-accommodations statute, so the practical operation of those protections is not sourced here.

Whether the 2022 self-determination rule extends to state-issued documents beyond birth certificates is not specified in the sources; the driver's licence and state ID marker is governed separately by the 2019 motor-vehicle policy.
